word_order: SVO | Subjects precede verbs and objects follow verbs in examples such as 'Travellers are strongly advised' and 'They made them stand out'.
punctuation_present: sometimes — as observed in the sample
target_language_risks: Missing future context can cause wrong case/gender/article choice in German because articles and case marking often depend on the noun that follows.
Verb placement: German subordinate clauses are verb-final; translating an English fragment too early can produce wrong word order or incorrect auxiliary placement.
Phrasal verbs and particle verbs split by later material (e.g. 'take ... up') will be mistranslated if split before the particle/object is seen.
Prepositional-phrase attachment ambiguity and relative-clause boundaries often require following words to choose correct German structure.
Named-entity fragmentation (e.g. 'Berlin, Germany') or numeric tokens split across segments can produce incorrect translations or formatting.
notes_for_prompt_writer: Prefer emitting segments at strong sentence boundaries (period, semicolon, question mark) or after clause-final connectors when the clause is complete. Avoid splitting immediately after abbreviations (Dr., e.g.) or numeric commas, and do not emit a segment that ends with a subordinating conjunction, preposition, or a verb that expects an object/particle. Keep noun phrases with their modifiers and verb + object (or verb + particle) together when possible to preserve German case and word order.
